- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.67) in recent days, reduce forecast overshoot by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to short-term momentum.  
- If sentiment is bearish (≤ 0.33) or mixed, increase downward bias in forecast, especially if recent prices are trending up — avoid “false optimism” in bullish sentiment.  
- When model forecast peaks sharply after a spike, reduce the peak by 5–15% to account for mean reversion or volatility decay.  
- If true outcome is consistently below forecast for 3–5 days, apply a “mean reversion” correction: subtract 1–3% from next forecast to avoid overestimating continuation.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is neutral or mixed, align forecast mean with recent 7–14 day average to reduce horizon bias.  
- If sentiment turns negative after a spike, reduce forecast slope downward — avoid “sustained overcorrection” after sharp moves.  
- If forecast is consistently 5–10% above true outcome over 3–5 days, apply a “sentiment-adjusted downward bias” rule: subtract 2–5% per day of negative sentiment.
